title: Becker muscular dystrophy associated with sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a paediatric patient: a case report
case_prompt:
A 10-year-old boy was referred for cardiac screening after being diagnosed with Becker muscular dystrophy. He initially presented to the neuromuscular clinic with exercise-induced muscular pain and markedly elevated serum creatine kinase levels (2495 U/L). Neuromuscular examination showed bilateral calf hypertrophy, decreased ankle joint range of motion, and very mild weakness of hip abduction and adduction (Medical Research Council grade 4), with preserved strength elsewhere. Genetic testing confirmed an in-frame deletion of exons 45–48 of the dystrophin gene.

The patient was asymptomatic from a cardiovascular standpoint, and cardiovascular examination findings were unremarkable. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with normal PR interval and QRS axis, voltage criteria for biventricular hypertrophy, and pathological Q waves in the inferolateral leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed asymmetric septal hypertrophy, predominantly of the anteroseptal wall extending toward the apex, with a maximal mid-septal wall thickness of 18 mm. The left ventricular cavity was small and globally hyperdynamic, with normal diastolic performance, normal left atrial size, and no systolic anterior motion or resting outflow tract obstruction.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed asymmetric hypertrophy of the basal and mid interventricular septum (maximal wall thickness, 18 mm) without outflow tract obstruction and demonstrated patchy late gadolinium enhancement within the hypertrophied myocardium.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Unlikely to be typical BMD cardiomyopathy — “Myocardial involvement is less frequent among patients with BMD than in those with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and most commonly takes the form of a dilated cardiomyopathy.”  
2. Consider inborn errors of metabolism — “…combination of neuromuscular symptoms and left ventricular hypertrophy should prompt a search for alternative differential diagnoses, including inborn errors of metabolism such as glycogen storage diseases or, in an adult, Fabry disease.”  
3. Familial cardiac sarcoidosis possibility — “The only family member with a history of cardiac disease was the maternal grandfather, who was reported to have undergone a heart transplant due to cardiac sarcoidosis…”  
4. Support for sarcomeric HCM — “Genetic testing for HCM-causing mutations was performed on a 104-gene panel… and identified likely pathogenic variants in heterozygosis in the beta-myosin heavy chain gene (MYH7 c.2701G>C; p.Ala901Pro).”  
5. Exclusion of MYH7 congenital myopathy — “His neuromuscular presentation is in keeping with BMD with no features suggestive of MHY7 gene-related congenital myopathy.”
